source.notes: No official marking scheme is published with this paper; questions carry no official answer. Genuine ICSE 2026 board examination paper from the CISCE Archive Library bundle 'ICSE-2026-MAIN-1.zip'; every page is footed 'T26 522' (used as paperCode). Maximum Marks 80, Time allowed Two hours. Section A (Questions 1–2, 40 marks) is compulsory; Section B (Questions 3–8, 10 marks each) says 'Attempt any four questions', so the printed marks in this pack total 100 (40 + 6×10), as expected. Question 1's fifteen MCQ/assertion-reason items share one printed [15] (1 mark each). Question 2's [5] groups (ii), (iv) and (v) were split into 1-mark items; 2 (i) (diagram-based, four sub-parts) and 2 (iii) (matching) are kept whole. Section B items are kept at the roman-numeral level where marks are printed. Chemical subscripts, superscripts and ionic charges were rebuilt as Unicode from the PDF layout (small lowered/raised glyphs checked with pdfplumber) and flagged. Most reaction arrows in this paper are drawn as vector line + arrow-head graphics (one is a small image, one a Wingdings glyph, one a Cambria Math extensible arrow) and are absent from the text layer; they were rebuilt as '→' from their positions and flagged. The text layer contains a few Cyrillic look-alike 'С' letters in Q1 (v), normalised to Latin C and flagged. pdftotext -layout interleaves Q1 (viii)-(x) on page 5; raw mode was used there. The paper ends with a stray '`' character on page 16, ignored.
source.usage: Official CISCE board examination paper from the CISCE Archive Library (cisce.org/archive-library); question text reproduced for study with attribution and a link to the original. Figures are not reproduced.

Alex was given a solution of an unknown salt Y for analysis. He performed the following tests and recorded his observations:

• To the remaining solution he added a few drops of sodium hydroxide solution and obtained a pale blue precipitate.
Based on the observations made by Alex, identify:
(a) the anion and
(b) the cation present in salt Y.

Equal volumes of ammonia gas and chlorine gas are kept in two different containers under the same conditions of temperature and pressure.
Find the number of molecules contained in chlorine gas when the mass of ammonia is 34 g.
[Atomic weight: Cl=35.5, H=1, N=14]

Elements P, Q, and R are in the same period of the modern periodic table.
• P readily loses its one valence electron to form a stable ion.
• Q shares its electrons in bonding but does not form ions easily.
• R has high electronegativity.
Answer the following questions based on the above information:
(a) Which element would be most difficult to reduce among P, Q and R?
(b) Which element is expected to have the smallest atomic radius among P, Q and R?
(c) Arrange P, Q and R in order of decreasing ionization potential.

Lead nitrate, Copper, Hydrochloric acid, Lead oxide, Iron, Sodium carbonate, Copper carbonate, Chlorine

(Note: The chemicals may be used more than once, if needed.)
(a) Lead (II) carbonate
(b) Copper (II) chloride
(c) Iron (II) chloride

(b) Name a suitable catalyst which is used in the reaction.
(c) Write a balanced chemical equation for the above reaction.

(a) Name the gas collected.
(b) Which acid is formed when the gas collected by the chemist is dissolved directly in water?
(c) Why should we not dissolve this gas directly in water?

(b) Silver nitrate solution is not preferred as an electrolyte in the above process. Give a reason.
(c) Why is alternating current not used in the process?
(d) What is the observation at the anode?

(a) What was the error made by Anil while storing the acid?
(b) Why were brown fumes observed in the container?
(c) How can the yellowish tinge in the acid be removed?
